topic.examWeightHint: Unit 1 is one two-hour calculator paper of 100 marks, sat every Summer. Curve sketching is a long question late in the paper: 13 marks over four parts in Summer 2019 Q8, 13 marks over six parts in Summer 2025 Q11, and multi-part questions in Summer 2018 Q9, Summer 2022 Q10, Summer 2023 Q12 and Summer 2024 Q10. The parts run in a fixed order: where the curve meets the axes (2 or 3 marks, no calculus), the turning points (3 marks for a quadratic, 5 or 6 for a cubic), their nature (1 or 2 marks), the sketch (2 marks), and often an area afterwards. Schemes run M1 for the factorising or the derivative, W1 for each coordinate, and MW1 for the second-derivative test.
mustMemorise: Crossings first: y = 0 for the x-axis, x = 0 for the y-axis, and no calculus in either
Turning points: solve dy/dx = 0, then substitute that x into the curve for the height
Nature: d²y/dx² positive is a minimum, negative is a maximum
A cubic turns at most twice, and two turns mean one maximum and one minimum
The sign of the highest power decides which way the ends of the curve go
Every crossing and turning point is labelled on the sketch as a coordinate
onFormulaSheet: If y = axⁿ then dy/dx = naxⁿ⁻¹ (Unit 1 formula sheet, page 2)
notOnThisSpec: Quartics and higher powers: FM1-DIF-02 names quadratic and cubic sketching only
Transformations of graphs, so never a shifted or stretched copy of the printed curve
Cubics that are neither a product of three linear factors nor have x as a common factor (Teacher Guidance for FM1-DIF-02)

steps.working: Set $y = 0$: $x^2 - 6x + 5 = 0$, which factorises to $(x - 1)(x - 5) = 0$, so $x = 1$ or $x = 5$.
steps.decision: Every point on the x-axis has height zero, so the crossings are the solutions of the equation itself. No calculus belongs in this line.

options: Because a point on the x-axis has y = 0
Because the turning point sits on the x-axis
whyMenu.explain: The x-axis is the set of points with height zero, so putting y = 0 into the equation finds exactly where the curve touches it.

steps.working: Write the crossings as coordinates: $(1, 0)$ and $(5, 0)$.
steps.decision: The question asks where the curve meets the axis, and a place on the page needs two numbers. Bare values of x lose the accuracy mark.

steps.working: Set $x = 0$: $y = 5$, so the curve meets the y-axis at $(0, 5)$.
steps.decision: The constant term is the height at x = 0, so this crossing can be read straight off the equation once you know why.
The turning point is where the curve is momentarily level, and the gradient function is what tells you that. This is where calculus starts.

steps.working: Set the gradient to zero: $2x - 6 = 0$, so $x = 3$.
steps.decision: Solving the derivative gives only the x of the turning point. It says nothing yet about how high the curve is there.

steps.working: Substitute into the curve: $y = (3)^{2} - 6(3) + 5 = -4$, so the turning point is $(3, -4)$.
steps.decision: Into the curve, never into the derivative. The derivative is zero there by construction, so it would hand back a height of nothing.

options: Because the height comes from y, not from the gradient
Because both give the same number
whyMenu.explain: dy/dx is zero at the turning point, so substituting into it returns 0 whatever the curve is. Only the original equation knows the height.

steps.working: Differentiate again: $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = 2$, which is positive, so $(3, -4)$ is a minimum.
steps.decision: A positive second derivative means the gradient is climbing through zero: down, level, up. That is a dip.

steps.working: Sketch: mark $(1, 0)$, $(5, 0)$, $(0, 5)$ and $(3, -4)$, then draw one U through them with the coefficient of $x^{2}$ positive.
steps.decision: Label every point you calculated. The sketch mark is for a picture that agrees with your own numbers, not for a neat curve.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Crossings $(1, 0)$, $(5, 0)$ and $(0, 5)$; turning point $(3, -4)$, a minimum because $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = 2$.

steps.working: The product is zero when any bracket is zero, so $x = 0$, $x = 5$ or $x = 8$, giving $(0, 0), (5, 0), (8, 0)$.
steps.decision: A factorised cubic hands you its crossings. Expanding first and then trying to factorise again would only make work.
The power rule needs separate terms, so the brackets have to come apart before you differentiate. Multiply the last two first, then bring in the x.
Each term on its own: multiply by the power, then step the power down.

steps.working: Set it to zero: $(3x - 20)(x - 2) = 0$, so $x = \frac{20}{3}$ or $x = 2$.
steps.decision: A cubic's derivative is a quadratic, so there are two answers here, not one. Finding only one is a sign that a factor has been dropped.
Both go back into the curve. The second one is a fraction, and it stays a fraction in the answer; the decimal is only for placing the point on the sketch.

steps.working: Second derivative: $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = 6x - 26$. At $x = 2$ it is $-14$, so $(2, 36)$ is a maximum. At $x = \frac{20}{3}$ it is $14$, so that point is a minimum.
steps.decision: Test each point separately. On a cubic the second derivative changes sign between them, which is why one of each always appears.

options: Because the second derivative is negative at one and positive at the other
Because the first x found is always the maximum
Because a cubic has two maxima
whyMenu.explain: The sign at the point is what names it. On this curve it is negative at the left-hand turn and positive at the right-hand one.

steps.working: Sketch: mark the three crossings, the maximum $(2, 36)$ and the minimum at about $(6.67, -14.81)$, then draw a curve rising away to the right.
steps.decision: The coefficient of x cubed is positive, so the curve comes up from the bottom left and leaves at the top right. Label every point.

items.stem:
Three checks on what this lesson is built from. None of them is the new method, so answer from what you already know.
Factorise $x^{2} + x - 12$.
items.skill: Factorise a quadratic with unit leading coefficient

options.feedback: The two numbers multiply to $-12$ and add to $+1$. That is the step a crossings question rests on.
Those multiply to $-12$ but add to $-1$, so the middle term would come out as $-x$.
Those multiply to $-12$ but add to $+4$. Check the sum as well as the product.

items.skill: Read the solutions from a factorised equation

options.feedback: Each bracket is set to zero in turn, and the sign flips as you solve it.
The signs inside the brackets have been copied straight out. Solving $x - 2 = 0$ gives $x = 2$, not $x = -2$.
That is the product of the two constants. A product is zero when one factor is zero, which gives two separate answers.

items.skill: Differentiate a quadratic term by term

options.feedback: Multiply by the power, step the power down, and the constant goes to zero.
The middle term $-6x$ has power 1, so its derivative is the number $-6$, with no $x$ left.
The constant $5$ differentiates to zero, so it does not appear in the gradient function at all.

items.stem: Where does the curve $y = (x - 4)(x + 7)$ meet the $x$-axis?
items.skill: Find the x-axis crossings of a factorised quadratic

options.feedback: Each bracket set to zero, then both answers written as coordinates.
The constants have been copied out of the brackets without solving. $x - 4 = 0$ gives $x = 4$ and $x + 7 = 0$ gives $x = -7$.
The algebra is right. The question asks where the curve meets the axis, which is a place, so each answer needs its $y$ value as well.

items.stem: The curve $y = x^{2} + 2x - 15$ has $\frac{dy}{dx} = 2x + 2$, which is zero at $x = -1$. What is the turning point?
items.skill: Find the height of a turning point

options.feedback: Substituting $-1$ into the curve gives $-16$.
That height came from substituting into $\frac{dy}{dx}$, which is zero at a turning point by definition. The height has to come from the curve.
Both numbers are right and they are the wrong way round. The value you solved for is the $x$, and the height you worked out is the $y$.

items.stem: At a turning point a curve has $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = 8$. What kind of point is it?
items.skill: Name a turning point from the sign of the second derivative

options.feedback: A positive second derivative means the gradient is rising through zero, so the curve falls to the point and climbs away.
The test runs the other way: positive is a minimum and negative is a maximum. Picture the gradient going down, level, up.

options.text: It cannot be decided without the sketch
options.feedback: The second derivative settles it on its own, which is why the examiners ask for it rather than for a drawing.

items.stem: Where does the curve $y = (x + 1)(x - 3)(x - 6)$ meet the $x$-axis?
items.skill: Find the crossings of a factorised cubic

options.feedback: Three brackets, three crossings, each written as a coordinate.
The origin has been added out of habit. Putting $x = 0$ into this cubic gives $y = 18$, so the curve passes well above $(0, 0)$.
Each constant has been copied out with its printed sign. Solving $x + 1 = 0$ gives $x = -1$, and $x - 3 = 0$ gives $x = 3$.

parts.stem:
The curve $y = -2x^{2} + 8x$ has a turning point at $(2, 8)$.
Determine whether it is a maximum or a minimum.

options.text: A maximum, because $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = -4$, which is negative
options.feedback: A negative second derivative means the gradient is falling through zero, so the curve peaks there.

options.text: A minimum, because $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = -4$, which is negative
options.feedback: The second derivative is right and the conclusion is reversed. Negative names a maximum, positive names a minimum.

options.text: A minimum, because the turning point is above the $x$-axis
options.feedback: Height above the axis says nothing about which way a curve turns. Only the sign of the second derivative decides it.

scheme.for: $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = -4$, which is negative, so the point is a maximum

hints: Differentiate twice.
Negative names a maximum; positive names a minimum.
parts.workedSolution:
$\frac{dy}{dx} = -4x + 8$, so $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = -4$.
That is negative, so $(2, 8)$ is a maximum.

Set $y = 0$: $x^{2} = 4$, so $x = 2$ or $x = -2$, giving $(-2, 0)$ and $(2, 0)$.
Set $x = 0$: $y = -4$, giving $(0, -4)$.
Plot those three points and draw one smooth U through them.

findTheMistake.stem: Saoirse was asked to find the coordinates of each point where the curve $y = x^{2} - 10x + 21$ meets the $x$-axis. Her working:
studentWorking: The curve meets the x-axis at (5, 0)
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong:
Line 2 is where it goes astray. Differentiating finds where the curve is level, which is the turning point, not where it meets the axis.
The crossings come from setting $y$ itself to zero and factorising: this quadratic gives $(x - 3)(x - 7) = 0$.
Everything after line 2 is correct arithmetic on the wrong equation, and line 5 also reports one point where there are two.
correction: The curve meets the x-axis at (3, 0) and (7, 0)
findTheMistake.feedback: The differentiating itself is accurate, and the same line would earn its mark in the next part of a real question. Here the word to read is "meets": a crossing is where the height is zero, so set $y = 0$ and factorise. The crossings are $(3, 0), (7, 0)$, and $x = 5$ is the turning point, which sits halfway between them.

The curve meets the x-axis at (0, 0), (-2, 0), (3, 0) and (5, 0)

correction: so the curve meets the x-axis at (-2, 0), (3, 0) and (5, 0) only
findTheMistake.feedback: Test a habit before trusting it: put x = 0 into the brackets. If the height is not 0, the origin is not a crossing. The Summer 2023 report saw (0, 0) added just like this.

prompts.prompt: How do you find where a curve meets the $x$-axis?
prompts.answer: Set $y = 0$ and solve the equation, usually by factorising; each solution is the $x$ of a point whose $y$ is zero.

prompts.prompt: How do you find where a curve meets the $y$-axis?
prompts.answer: Set $x = 0$ and work out the height; for a polynomial that is the constant term.

prompts.prompt: How do you find a turning point?
prompts.answer: Solve $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$ for $x$, then substitute that $x$ into the curve to find the height.

prompts.prompt: You have solved $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$. What do you substitute that value into?
prompts.answer: The curve itself, never the derivative: the derivative is zero there by definition, so it would give a height of zero every time.

prompts.prompt: How does the second derivative name a turning point?
prompts.answer: A positive second derivative at the point means a minimum, and a negative one means a maximum.

prompts.prompt: How many turning points can a cubic have, and of which kinds?
prompts.answer: Two at most, and when there are two they are always one maximum and one minimum, because the derivative is a quadratic.

prompts.prompt: What must be written on a sketch for the final mark?
prompts.answer: The coordinates of every axis crossing and of every turning point, labelled on the curve.

findings.asked: Intercepts, turning points, then sketch a cubic.
findings.wentWrong: Some differentiated in the intercepts part; sketches did not extend to all relevant regions.
findings.rule: Intercepts: set y = 0 and x = 0 - no calculus yet.

findings.wentWrong: x-values given instead of coordinates; differentiation in the intercept part; errors in the y-value of a turning point; two maxima found without noticing the contradiction; sketches missing labelled points.
findings.rule: A cubic has one maximum and one minimum - a contradiction means an error.

findings.asked: Turning points and nature, sketch, then area.
findings.wentWrong: Some wrote the derivatives without knowing what to do; some confused the axis crossings with turning points; a maximum below the x-axis confused the sketch.
findings.rule: Plot the turning points you found and draw the curve through them regardless of where they sit.

findings.asked: Where a cubic meets the axes; expand; turning points; nature; sketch.
findings.wentWrong: (0, 0) was added as an intercept out of habit; brackets omitted in expansion; sketches sometimes had a maximum below a minimum or were not attempted.
findings.rule: Read the intercepts from the factorised form; the sketch must match your own results.

findings.wentWrong: Differentiating in part (i) again, which then spoiled the sketch shape.
findings.rule: Part (i) is intercepts; calculus starts at the turning points.

findings.asked: Quadratic: intercepts, turning point, sketch, area.
findings.wentWrong: Some differentiated for the intercepts; the turning point was not written as a coordinate; a few drew cubics; key points unlabelled.
findings.rule: Label intercepts and the turning point as coordinates on the sketch.

insight.ruleToRemember: Intercepts from y = 0 and x = 0 (no calculus); turning points from dy/dx = 0 with nature from the second derivative; the sketch must pass through your intercepts and turning points with all of them labelled as coordinates.
